newsitem.title: GERMANY: German venture capital mkt seen dwarfed by rivals.
newsitem.headline: German venture capital mkt seen dwarfed by rivals.

text.p: Germany's venture capital market is dwarfed by comparison with rival financial centres and will remain so unless it changes its tax system, reforms its stock market and gets the right knowhow, the designated chief of Deutsche Bank AG said on Tuesday.

The country also lacks an equity culture and there is a general aversion to taking risk -- two factors which have ensured that the volume of venture capital invested in Germany is far smaller than in the United States, Britain and France, Rolf Breuer told a conference in Frankfurt.

"A functioning venture capital market is an essential part of a financial centre," said Breuer, a management board member of Deutsche who is due to take over as chief executive of Germany's largest bank in May.
Lack of money was not the problem, Breuer said, noting that state development aid for new businesses was relatively generous.
Venture capital investment refers to providing funds for new firms in return for a shareholding and a say in management.
It is risky and the only return it offers is the income from the eventual sale of the stake. While most start-ups fail, the proceeds from the ones that succeed can be substantial.
At the end of 1995 Germany had about six billion marks of private capital invested in 3,000 companies starting up, giving an average of investment of two million marks per firm.

The British market is three times larger, the French market one-and-a-half times and some 43 billion dollars of venture capital is invested in the U.S., with an average of 11 to 12 million dollars per company.
Breuer said the German market was underdeveloped because of shortcomings of investors as well as entrepreneurs.

"We lack an equity culture. Only five percent of Germans own shares. If they don't even touch a blue chip which is liquid and whose price you can read in the newspaper every day then one doesn't even need to begin talking about venture capital."

While last November's flotation of telephone giant Deutsche Telekom AG had familiarised many Germans with the option of investing in shares, it was too soon to tell if the offering had given the equity market a big push, Breuer said.
He called on the government to remove tax barriers to the creation of pension funds which in other countries are the main investors in venture capital.

In addition taxes on the sale of share stakes -- the only remuneration for investors who put their money in companies starting up -- should be removed, thereby creating an incentive to provide venture capital, Breuer said.
Meanwhile better lines of communication were needed between investors and entrepreneurs to ensure the necessary exchange of knowhow on developing new products and marketing them.
Another problem is that Germany's Mittelstand -- small and medium-sized businesses -- often shun venture capital because they do not want outsiders to have a say in their business, Breuer said.

Germany must also continue to reform its stock market to boost the number of initial price offerings, which in other countries are a popular way for venture capital investors to obtain the return on their outlays, Breuer said.
